correctness.rationale: The initial singleton colours propagate distance-sphere membership to all vertices by round k, so the colour at k+1 gives the joint vector of each neighbour's landmark-overlap displacements as a multiset. Swaps (a,b) with a,b both in X can be added to an odd moment without changing it: their terms cancel in reversed pairs and the diagonal terms vanish. For odd |U| the all-s_i monomial in the resulting polynomial has coefficient (-1)^|U| n=-n. For even |U| the squared displacement at j has linear coefficient 1-2t_j on Boolean inputs and the other |U|-1 factors contribute a minus sign, producing -(n-2k) after summing over b. All other terms involve strict subsets of U, so induction at the same colour round determines every intersection count. Boolean inversion recovers the atom profile. The product of symmetric groups on the atoms acts transitively on each profile and fixes all marks. Conversely even the full coloured-graph automorphism subgroup cannot mix colours, so no classification of Johnson automorphisms is needed. Each atom contributes an independent binomial choice or an independent truncated geometric series for counting profiles. No marks gives one orbit, and the argument includes k=1 and the all-marked case; set complementation transports k>n/2 with the asserted bound.
residual_risks: At n=2k the coefficient for even subsets vanishes and the argument makes no claim about that case. The bound is not claimed sharp.

evidence: The hierarchy theorem characterizes (m+1)-Tinhofer by orbit equality for up to m marks. The general complexity paper concerns individualization goals such as discreteness, amenability, compactness or refinability. The Johnson theorem of Arvind et al. is rank two.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The general results cover more graphs as frameworks or algorithms, not as a proof that higher-rank Johnson graphs satisfy the required orbit-equality hypothesis for all marks. The rank-two theorem has full mark quantification but cannot cover higher rank.

evidence: The two-anchor theorem gives data for two landmarks at a time. Pairwise intersections and single overlaps do not in general determine a multi-landmark Boolean profile. The submitted odd-neighbour moments explicitly extract arbitrary higher-order intersection counts.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Applying the two-mark result to every pair is not a derivation of the all-mark claim; nor does compact/partial-Tinhofer terminology replace the need to prove the higher-rank hypotheses. No dominating theorem deriving the unrestricted profile and time bound was found in the inspected material.

evidence: Tinhofer (or the arbitrary-individualization orbit equality criterion) is the relevant reformulation of the qualitative conclusion. The closest Resultary theorem obtains orbit equality by k+1 for two marks, with the atom profiles specialized to four zones.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The same-graph partition equality yields a Tinhofer corollary via the general hierarchy criterion; that criterion does not prove the equality for the Johnson family. The bound concerns synchronous counting-refinement rounds, not the number of marks in a partial Tinhofer criterion.

value.rationale: Johnson graphs are a natural highly symmetric test family for individualized refinement. The theorem handles all landmark interactions at once (not just distance vectors or pairs), gives exact orbit sizes and counts, and bounds the number of rounds independently of the number of marks. The use of odd moments to recover higher-order intersections, with an explicit obstruction to the method on the middle layer, is a useful structural mechanism rather than a finite census or a rank-two restatement.
